entry: U.S. Marine veteran and assassin of [[John F. Kennedy]]. On November 22, 1963, Oswald shot Kennedy from a window of the Texas School Book Depository in [[Dallas]], then killed police officer J. D. Tippit and was arrested in a theater. He denied the charges, claiming he was a patsy. Two days later, nightclub owner Jack Ruby shot Oswald on live television at Dallas Police Headquarters. The Warren Commission concluded in September 1964 that Oswald and Ruby had acted alone. Public-opinion polls have shown that most Americans still doubt the official version, and the assassination has spawned numerous conspiracy theories.

Singaporean politician and barrister, first prime minister of Singapore from 1959 to 1990. He co-founded the People's Action Party (PAP) in 1954 and led it to its first electoral victory in 1959. Singapore merged with Malaya, Sarawak and Sabah to form [[Malaysia]] in 1963, but was expelled in 1965 and became independent. Lee oversaw economic reforms and urban development, promoting meritocracy, multiracialism and anti-corruption. His administration is often characterized as an illiberal democracy that restricted press freedoms, public assembly, labor activism and [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]]. He is widely regarded as instrumental in developing Singapore's economy, education system, foreign policy and public housing, and as the founding father of modern Singapore. He remained in the cabinet as senior minister until 2004. After his death, approximately 1.7 million people paid their respects at tribute sites across the country.

American actor known for hard-boiled roles and a bass voice. Marvin was a decorated [[United States Marine Corps|Marine]] who served as a scout sniper with the 4th Marine Division in the Pacific during World War II. Initially typecast as a villain, he later gained prominence playing anti-heroes. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Cat Ballou* (1965), a comic Western in which he played a dual role. Other films include *The Big Heat* (1953), *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* (1962) and *The Dirty Dozen* (1967).

American inventor and electrical engineer, an early pioneer of electronics. In 1908 he invented the Audion, a three-element triode [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]] and the first practical electronic [[Amplifier|amplifier]]. The device helped start the Electronic Age and enabled the electronic oscillator, which made radio broadcasting and long-distance telephone lines possible and led to talking motion pictures. De Forest held more than 300 patents worldwide, but his career was turbulent. He boasted that he made, then lost, four fortunes, was involved in several major patent lawsuits, and was tried and acquitted of mail fraud. He received the 1922 IRE Medal of Honor, the 1923 Franklin Institute Elliott Cresson Medal and the 1946 American Institute of Electrical Engineers Edison Medal.

Segmented parasitic or predatory worm of the subclass Hirudinea, in the phylum Annelida. Leeches are closely related to the oligochaetes, including the [[Earthworm|earthworm]], and have soft, muscular bodies that can lengthen and contract. Most have suckers at both ends. The best-known species, such as the medicinal leech *Hirudo medicinalis*, are hematophagous and feed on [[Blood|blood]], first secreting the peptide hirudin to prevent clotting. The majority of leeches live in freshwater habitats, and a minority are predatory, mostly preying on small invertebrates. Leeches were used in [[Medicine|medicine]] from ancient times until the 19th century to draw blood. Today they are used in microsurgery and to treat joint diseases such as epicondylitis and [[Osteoarthritis|osteoarthritis]], while hirudin is used as an anticoagulant drug. The word leech is also used for a person who takes without giving.

City and metropolitan borough in West Yorkshire, England, and the largest settlement in Yorkshire. Built around the River Aire, Leeds was a market town in the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]] and became a major center of the wool trade in the 17th and 18th centuries. It was awarded a city charter in 1893 by [[Queen Victoria]]. During the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] it developed as a mill town known for its flax industry, iron foundries, engineering and printing. Its economy is among the most diverse of the UK's main employment centers, and the city is home to five universities and the Leeds United football club. The city had 536,280 residents, while the larger City of Leeds district had 812,000 (2021 census).

Biennial vegetable in the onion family, a cultivar of *Allium ampeloprasum*. The edible part is a bundle of leaf sheaths, sometimes called a stem or stalk. The genus *Allium* also includes the [[Onion|onion]], [[Garlic|garlic]], shallot, scallion and chives. The name leek developed from the Old English word *lēac*, which also gave modern English the name for garlic. Leeks are more cold-tolerant than other cultivated alliums and can be harvested up to six months after planting. They have a mild, onion-like taste. The white base and light green parts are typically eaten, while the dark green portion is usually discarded or used for stock. Leeks may be boiled, fried or eaten raw in [[Salad|salads]]. In France, whole boiled leeks served cold with vinaigrette are popular.

Range of political ideologies that favor social equality and egalitarianism. Left-wing politics typically concerns those perceived as disadvantaged and seeks to reduce unjustified inequalities. The left-right terms date from the [[French Revolution]], when delegates opposed to the royal veto sat to the left of the presiding officer. The term now usually applies to movements critical of [[Capitalism|capitalism]], including socialism, anarchism, communism and Marxism. Social democracy and social liberalism are considered center-left. Critics argue that communist regimes produced authoritarian governance and economic inefficiency, while debate continues over whether expansive government intervention reduces economic dynamism.

Political ideology combining [[Left-wing politics|left-wing politics]] with [[Populism|populist]] rhetoric. It often opposes the Establishment and speaks for the masses against economic monopolies, emphasizing economic democracy, social justice and skepticism of [[Globalization|globalization]]. Unlike right-wing populists, left-wing populist parties tend to support minority rights and a nationality not defined by ethnic particularism. In the [[United States]], [[Bernie Sanders]] is an example. Since the 2010s the label has also been applied to left-liberal movements, and in the 2020s left-liberal economic populism appealing to the [[Working class|working class]] has been prominent in some countries, such as South Korea under Lee Jae-myung.

Study of how law has evolved and why it has changed. Legal history is closely connected to the development of civilizations and to social history. Twentieth-century historians viewed legal institutions as complex systems of rules, players and symbols that interact with society, and they used statistical methods to analyze case outcomes. Ancient Egyptian law, dating to 3000 BC, was based on the concept of *Ma'at*. By the 22nd century BC, the Sumerian ruler Ur-Nammu had formulated the first extant law code, and [[Hammurabi]] later codified Babylonian law on stelae. Roman law, systematized in the [[Corpus Juris Civilis]] under [[Justinian I]], influenced [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] traditions in continental Europe, while [[Common law|common law]] spread through the [[British Empire]] to India, Malaysia, Singapore and Hong Kong.

Ancient Chinese school of political philosophy, or *fajia*. Legalists generally viewed most people, or at least the elite, as self-interested, and emphasized equality under the law, administrative methods and regulation. They opposed the [[Confucianism|Confucians]], who favored cultivated virtue, and the Mohists, who favored universal love. Legalist ideas were first adopted in the state of [[Qin dynasty|Qin]] under the reforms of [[Shang Yang]] in the 4th century BCE, which helped Qin conquer China and establish its first imperial dynasty. [[Han Fei]] is considered by many the greatest Legalist thinker. Later rulers, distancing themselves from Qin's brutality, adopted Confucianism as the official ideology, but the Legalist bureaucratic apparatus was kept by the [[Han dynasty]] and remained a profound influence on Chinese statecraft. The label was a later bibliographic category, and some recent scholars regard it as inaccurate.

Genre of [[Folklore|folklore]] consisting of a narrative about human actions believed or perceived to have taken place in history. Legends concern human beings as main characters and do not necessarily have supernatural origins, which distinguishes them from [[Myth|myths]]. The [[Brothers Grimm]] defined legend as "folktale historically grounded." Many legends are never entirely believed by their audiences but never resolutely doubted, and they may include [[Miracle|miracles]] and change over time. The word entered English c. 1340 from Old French, derived from the Medieval Latin *legenda*. Legends often reaffirm values commonly held by the group to whose tradition they belong. Urban legends are a modern example.

Supernatural entity described in [[Folklore|folklore]] that has not been scientifically shown to exist. Some legendary creatures originated in traditional mythology and were believed to be real, such as [[Dragon|dragons]], [[Griffin|griffins]] and [[Unicorn|unicorns]]. Others were based on garbled accounts of travelers' tales, such as the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary. Hybrid beasts are called [[Chimera (mythology)|chimeras]]. In classical tales, monsters such as the Cyclops and the Minotaur appear so that heroes can destroy them, emphasizing the heroes' greatness. In medieval bestiaries, animals were included regardless of biological reality and carried symbolic meanings. The unicorn was a metaphor for Christ, and the dragon was used to denote sin in general.

Form of atypical pneumonia caused by *Legionella* bacteria, most often *Legionella pneumophila*. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, high fever and muscle pains, usually beginning 2–10 days after exposure. *Legionella* is found naturally in fresh water and can contaminate hot water tanks, hot tubs and [[Cooling tower|cooling towers]]. Infection typically occurs by breathing in mist that contains the bacteria, and the disease does not usually spread directly between people. No [[Vaccine|vaccine]] is available, so prevention depends on maintaining water systems. Treatment commonly uses [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]. The disease is named after a 1976 outbreak at an American Legion convention in [[Philadelphia]].

Deliberative assembly that holds legal authority to make laws and exercise political oversight. Legislatures may exist at national, subnational, local or supranational levels, such as the [[European Parliament]]. They are among a state's principal institutions, typically contrasted with the [[Executive (government)|executive]] and judicial institutions. Laws enacted by legislatures are called primary legislation. Legislatures may also perform oversight, budgetary and representative functions, and they may be unicameral, bicameral or multicameral. The most common types are parliaments, which fuse executive and legislative powers and whose government is accountable to the legislature, and congresses, which operate under the [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]]. Communist states have had supreme state organs of power that centralize all state powers under a doctrine of unified power.

Brand of plastic construction toys made by the Lego Group, a privately held company based in Billund, Denmark. Lego consists of interlocking plastic bricks made of ABS, along with [[Gear|gears]], minifigures and other parts, that can be assembled into vehicles, buildings and working [[Robotics|robots]]. The company began in 1932 as a carpenter's workshop making wooden toys, and its name derives from the Danish phrase *leg godt* ("play well"). It began producing interlocking bricks in 1949, based on a design by English toymaker Hilary Page, and the modern brick design was developed in 1958. Annual brick production averages about 36 billion. As of July 2015, 600 billion Lego parts had been produced. Lego is the largest toy manufacturer in the world by sales, and the brand includes films, games and ten Legoland amusement parks.

Plant of the pea family [[Fabaceae|Fabaceae]], or the fruit or seeds of such a plant. Legumes produce a dry fruit that usually splits along two seams. Most have symbiotic nitrogen-fixing rhizobia bacteria in root nodules, and some of the fixed nitrogen becomes available to later crops, so legumes are important in crop rotation. Grown mainly for human food, legumes are also used as livestock forage and green manure. Seeds harvested solely for drying are called pulses and include [[Bean|beans]], [[Lentil|lentils]], [[Chickpea|chickpeas]] and [[Pea|peas]]. The family is the third-largest land plant family by number of species, with some 19,000 known species.

City and unitary authority, county town of Leicestershire, in the East Midlands of England (pop., 2025: 383,116). Leicester developed from the Roman town of Ratae Corieltauvorum, was later settled by the [[Anglo-Saxons|Anglo-Saxons]], and was captured by the [[Vikings|Vikings]]. After the death of Simon de Montfort in 1265 the town passed to the House of Lancaster. Richard III spent his last days in the town before his death at the Battle of Bosworth and was buried there in 1485. He was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015. Known in the Victorian age for hosiery and shoe manufacturing, Leicester gained city status in 1919.

Norse explorer, thought to have been the first European to set foot on continental America. According to the sagas of Icelanders, he established a Norse settlement at [[Vinland]], usually interpreted as coastal North America. Some speculation links his settlement to the Norse remains at L'Anse aux Meadows in [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]], Canada. He was the son of Erik the Red, who founded the first Norse settlement in [[Greenland]], where Leif was raised. After his voyage and his father's death, he became chief of the Greenland settlement. He was known as Leif the Lucky for rescuing shipwrecked sailors and converting Greenland to Christianity. The sagas, thought to have been written around 1200, contain sometimes conflicting accounts and are generally regarded as literature rather than purely historical records. His voyage preceded sustained European contact by about half a millennium before [[Christopher Columbus]].

City in Saxony, Germany, the state's most populous city (pop., 2025: 633,592). A trade city since at least the time of the [[Holy Roman Empire]], Leipzig has hosted a trade fair dating back to 1190. It was a center of publishing from 1764 to 1945. Events in Leipzig in 1989, beginning with demonstrations at St. Nicholas Church, played a significant role in precipitating the fall of communism in Europe. The city is home to one of Europe's oldest universities. [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Bach]], [[Felix Mendelssohn]] and [[Richard Wagner]] lived and worked there. Leipzig Hauptbahnhof is Europe's largest railway station by floor area.

Free time apart from work, job hunting, domestic chores and education, and from necessities such as eating and sleeping. Leisure is also defined as a quality of experience that emphasizes perceived freedom and choice and is pursued for its own sake. Thorstein Veblen described it as "nonproductive consumption of time." [[Recreation]] differs from leisure in being a purposeful activity that includes the experience of leisure. Economists treat leisure time as valuable to a person, as they do wages. Leisure was historically a privilege of the [[Upper class|upper class]], but opportunities for leisure expanded dramatically in the mid-to-late 19th century, starting in Great Britain. The concept of leisure as a human right appears in article 24 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]].

Small rodent of the Arctic [[Tundra|tundra]], related to [[Vole|voles]] and [[Muskrat|muskrats]] in the subfamily *Arvicolinae*. Lemmings measure about 13–18 cm and feed mostly on mosses and grasses, and they are a primary prey source for most Arctic carnivores. They do not hibernate and live in tunnel systems beneath the snow in winter. Their populations boom and then disperse, and the Norway and West Siberian lemmings are among the few vertebrates whose fluctuations are chaotic. Lemmings are conspicuously colored and behave aggressively toward predators, a defense thought to be a warning display. A longstanding myth claims they commit mass suicide by jumping off cliffs.

Yellow fruit of a small evergreen tree, *Citrus × limon*, in the family Rutaceae. A true lemon is a hybrid of the [[Citron|citron]] and the bitter orange. Its origins are uncertain, but it may have originated in northeastern India during the 1st millennium BC. Lemons reached Europe near southern Italy no later than the 2nd century AD. The first substantial cultivation in Europe began in [[Genoa]] in the mid-15th century, and [[Christopher Columbus]] brought seeds to [[Hispaniola]] in 1493. Lemon juice is about 5–6% [[Citric acid|citric acid]], giving it a sour taste, and it is used in drinks such as lemonade. In 1747 the English physician James Lind experimented with adding lemon juice to the diets of seamen suffering from [[Scurvy|scurvy]], before vitamin C was known. World production was 23 million tonnes in 2024, led by India and Mexico with 31% of the total.

Wet-nosed primate endemic to the island of Madagascar. Lemurs are divided into eight families and about 100 living species. Most are small, with large eyes and long tails, and they usually live in trees and are active at night. They evolved independently from [[Monkey|monkeys]] and [[Ape|apes]]. Living lemurs range from the mouse lemur, at about 30 g, to the indri, at 9 kg. Since humans arrived on the island about 2,000 years ago, more than a dozen species of giant lemurs have become extinct. Lemurs are generally the most social strepsirrhine primates. The IUCN considers them the world's most endangered mammals, noting that as of 2013 up to 90% of species face the threat of extinction within the next 20 to 25 years. Ring-tailed lemurs are an iconic flagship species.

River in the Russian Far East, the easternmost of Siberia's three great rivers flowing into the Arctic Ocean. The Lena is 4,294 km long and drains 2,490,000 sq km, making it the 11th-longest river in the world and the longest river entirely within Russia. Permafrost underlies its whole catchment and is continuous in over 75 percent of the basin. The river flows north past [[Yakutsk]] and widens into a delta of 30,000 sq km that merges into the Laptev Sea. The Lena is navigable for 3,540 km. Gold is washed from the sands of its tributaries, and mammoth tusks have been dug out of the delta.
